result.summary: Patroclus begs Achilles to let him fight in his armour, and Achilles agrees but warns him to return once the ships are safe. Patroclus routs the Trojans and kills Sarpedon, but Apollo strikes him down and Euphorbus and Hector kill him.

scenes.title: Patroclus pleads with Achilles
scenes.summary: Patroclus weeps and asks to wear Achilles' armour. Achilles agrees, but tells him to save the ships and then come back. Meanwhile Ajax is hard pressed.
scenes.stakes: Patroclus risks his life by taking Achilles' place, and Achilles risks his honour and his friend.

scenes.title: Ship burns; Myrmidons arm
scenes.summary: Hector cuts Ajax's spear and the Trojans fire a ship. Achilles tells Patroclus to arm, and the Myrmidon captains are listed.
scenes.stakes: The fleet is burning, and the Greeks risk being cut off from any way home.

scenes.title: Achilles' prayer to Jove
scenes.summary: Achilles exhorts the Myrmidons and prays to Jove for Patroclus. Jove grants only half of it.
scenes.stakes: Patroclus's safe return depends on the prayer, and Jove refuses it.

scenes.title: Patroclus routs the Trojans
scenes.summary: The Myrmidons swarm out and put out the fire. Many chieftains kill their men, and Patroclus drives the Trojans back across the trench.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans risk rout and death; Hector must flee.

scenes.title: Death of Sarpedon
scenes.summary: Patroclus kills Sarpedon after Jove yields to Juno. A fight over the body follows, and Apollo carries it away.
scenes.stakes: Sarpedon faces fated death; Patroclus ignores Achilles' warning.

scenes.title: Patroclus falls
scenes.summary: Apollo repels Patroclus at the wall and disarms him. Euphorbus wounds him and Hector kills him, and Patroclus foretells Hector's death.
scenes.stakes: Patroclus loses his life; Hector will soon face Achilles.

alias_notes.explanation: The text once uses the Greek name for Jove.

notable_quotes.reason: Patroclus's famous accusation that Achilles was born of sea and cliffs.
Dying Patroclus foretells Hector's death at Achilles' hands.

analysis.text: Pride and fate meet here: Patroclus ignores Achilles' limits and is destroyed by the gods. His death sets up Achilles' return to battle.
The Homeric similes drawn from herding, farming and woodcutting reflect the world of the poem's audience.

legacy.text: The death of Sarpedon was shown in Greek vase painting, notably the Euphronios krater.
The film Troy (2004) adapts Patroclus's death in Achilles' armour, though it makes him Achilles' cousin.

fun_facts.text: The Euphronios krater, showing Sleep and Death carrying Sarpedon, was returned to Italy by the Metropolitan Museum in 2008.

language_notes.text: "Baning" means ruining or poisoning; the phrase says Achilles' anger damages his own reputation.
Patroclus says Achilles must have been born of sea and rock, not human parents, because he is so hard-hearted.
"Which while they are fighting may hardly be" means men in constant battle rarely get a chance to rest.
"Creek nor grip" refers to inlets and gullies; "grip" is an old word for a small ditch or channel.
"Cars" is a misprint for "ears."
"Juno's thundering husband" is a periphrasis for Jove (the Greek Zeus), king of the gods.
Achilles wishes everyone dead except himself and Patroclus, so that they alone could capture Troy; "mantle that veils the brow of Troy" means its walls.
Traditional invocation of the Muses, goddesses of poetry and memory, who were thought to give the poet knowledge of events he did not witness.
Smiting the thighs is a gesture of strong emotion, such as distress or alarm.
Greaves are shin-guards; the cuirass is a breastplate. Both are pieces of armour.
Chiron was the wise centaur of Mount Pelion. Peleus is Achilles' father, so the spear is a family heirloom.
Xanthus and Balius are immortal horses born of a harpy and the west wind; they were a divine gift to Peleus.
Spercheius is a river god; 'streams from heaven' reflects the belief that rivers were sacred and Zeus-fed.
'Slayer of Argos' and 'giver of all good' are epithets of Mercury (the Greek Hermes). Diana is the Greek Artemis.
Ilithuia (Eileithyia) is the goddess who presides over childbirth.
"Straitly" is archaic for strictly or sternly; he gave them a strict charge.
Suckled on gall means raised on bitterness; the Myrmidons accuse Achilles of being bitter and pitiless from infancy.
"Serried" means pressed closely together in ranks.
Automedon is Achilles' charioteer and trusted companion, who leads alongside Patroclus.
Sulphur was burned or used for purification; cleansing the cup made it ritually pure for offering to the god.
Dodona was Jove's oracle in northern Greece; the Selli were its priests, whose unwashed feet and ground beds suggest ascetic austerity.
"Vouchsafe" means graciously grant; "aforetime" means previously.
"Squire" here means Patroclus as Achilles' attendant companion in war.
"Wayfarer" means a traveller on foot.
"With might and with main" is an old idiom meaning with all one's strength and effort.
"Ousted" means driven out or forced from a position.
The Chimaera was a fire-breathing monster of lion, goat and serpent parts, killed by Bellerophon. Here Amisodorus is said to have raised it.
Erebus is the dark region of the underworld through which the dead pass to Hades.
The immortal horses, Xanthus and Balius, were a wedding gift from the gods to Peleus, Achilles' father, and now draw Patroclus.
Jove's storm punishing crooked judges reflects the Greek belief that Zeus avenged injustice among men.
"Ungirdled tunics" means loose, unbelted tunics; it is a Homeric description of the Lycians, marking them as easy-moving, perhaps lightly armed.
"Mettle" means courage and spirit.
"Fastness" means a remote, secure stronghold or secluded place.
"Out of the jaws of death" means to rescue him from a death already fated for him.
A rain of blood was a portent; Jove weeps for his son with bloody drops falling from the sky.
"My name will haunt you" means Glaucus will carry the shame and blame forever if Sarpedon's armour is lost.
Refers to an earlier fight in which Teucer, the Greek archer, wounded Glaucus as he attacked the Greek wall.
"Contumely" means insulting, contemptuous treatment.
"Main stays" means chief supports, as the stays of a ship's mast; Sarpedon was a pillar of Troy's defence though a foreign ally.
"The two Ajaxes" are Ajax son of Telamon and the lesser Ajax son of Oileus, often fighting as a pair.
"Erewhile" is archaic for "formerly"; "Ilius" here means Troy.
"Mars robbed it of its force" means the war god ended the spear's quivering; the spear was spent.
Calling Meriones a "dancer" mocks his nimble dodging; Meriones was a Cretan, and the jibe implies he was light-footed but not a true fighter.
"The scales of Jove" refers to Jove weighing fates in a balance; the side that sinks is doomed to lose.
Death and Sleep (Thanatos and Hypnos) are twin divine brothers who convey the dead; ambrosia is the food of the gods, here used to preserve the body.
"Scatheless" means unharmed. The "bidding of the son of Peleus" is Achilles' order to return after relieving the ships.
The narrator addresses Patroclus directly as 'you' (apostrophe), a Homeric habit used for characters he feels sympathy for.
Phoebus is a title of Apollo, meaning 'bright' or 'radiant'.
The Scaean gates were the main gates of Troy's wall, facing the battlefield.
Apollo's riddling taunt: 'as much better than you as I am worse' means he is, in fact, far weaker than Hector, so Hector should be ashamed.
'Rule him' here means to master or overcome him; 'hurly-burly' later means the tumult of battle.
'Vaunt' means to boast or gloat over a defeated enemy.
'I ween' means 'I suppose'; 'straitly' means strictly.
The son of Leto is Apollo; Patroclus names fate, the god and Euphorbus before Hector, ranking Hector only third in his death.
The immortal steeds were a wedding gift from the gods to Peleus, Achilles' father; they now carry Automedon to safety.

context_notes.text: Patroclus is Achilles' closest companion. Achilles has withdrawn from the fighting because Agamemnon took his prize, the girl Briseis.
Menoetius is Patroclus' father and Peleus is Achilles' father. Phthia is their home region, and the Myrmidons are Achilles' followers.
Apollo supports the Trojans in the war, so Achilles warns Patroclus that the god may attack him.
Jove (the Greek Zeus) decides the outcome of battles; Ajax reads the broken spear as a sign that Jove favours the Trojans.
Burning the ships would strand the Achaeans at Troy, which is why Achilles finally yields and lets Patroclus fight.
Patroclus leaves behind Achilles' great spear because only Achilles can wield it, marking the limits of his borrowed power.
The Myrmidons are Achilles' own troops from Phthia. Fifty ships of fifty men gives a force of 2,500.
Thetis is Achilles' sea-goddess mother. Her gift of a chest packed for the voyage shows her foresight about his fate.
A cup reserved for Jove alone marks the special sanctity of this libation; pouring wine to a god was the usual form of prayer.
Jove's partial answer follows the Iliad's pattern: gods grant prayers only within the bounds of fate.
Patroclus wears Achilles' armour, so the Trojans mistake him for Achilles. They fear Achilles has ended his quarrel with Agamemnon.
Protesilaus' ship was the first Greek ship to land at Troy, and its owner was the first Greek killed. The Trojans were burning it.
This Ajax, son of Oileus, is the lesser Ajax, distinct from the great Ajax, son of Telamon, who appears in sentence 115.
Jove (the Greek Zeus) is Saturn's son and Juno's husband and brother. Sarpedon is his mortal son, so Jove grieves at his fate.
Death and Sleep are twin gods who carry the dead home. A mound and pillar were the standard honours of a hero's grave.
Automedon is Patroclus' charioteer. Pedasus was a mortal horse yoked as a side horse beside Achilles' immortal pair.
Apollo was a god of archery and healing, and he supported the Trojans and Lycians.
Sarpedon was a Lycian prince, a son of Jove, and a Trojan ally, which is why he is called an alien.
Mt. Ida, near Troy, was sacred to Jove, who often watches the war from its heights.
Phoebus is a name of Apollo, god of prophecy, archery and healing.
Apollo disguises himself as Asius, Hecuba's brother. Gods often take mortal shapes in the Iliad to advise or deceive.
Mars (the Greek Ares) is the god of war, so the comparison marks Patroclus' frenzy at its peak.
Patroclus wears Achilles' armour, lent so the Trojans would think Achilles had returned.
Hades is the underworld; in Homer the soul survives as a faint shade.

literary_notes.text: Patroclus' tears are compared to a spring falling down a cliff, which makes his grief seem copious and unceasing.
Achilles compares Patroclus to a clinging child, gently mocking him and showing his affection for his friend.
Patroclus calls Achilles the child of sea and cliffs, which turns his hardness into an image of inhuman nature.
The narrator tells us that Patroclus is asking for his own death, which Achilles and Patroclus do not know.
The sweat that "rained from every pore" emphasizes Ajax's exhaustion and shows how severe the pressure on the Greeks has become.
The poet addresses the Muses directly, lending the coming disaster solemnity and epic weight.
Ajax interprets the broken spear as the will of Jove, showing the gods directly steering human fortune.
The crest 'nodding menacingly' gives the helmet a threatening life of its own.
Patroclus' lack of Achilles' spear hints that he lacks Achilles' strength and may not survive.
The blood-reddened wolves compare the Myrmidons to predators, stressing their ferocity and hunger for battle after long idleness.
The tightly fitted stones of a wall compare to the packed Myrmidon ranks, conveying their solidity and strength.
The repeated "on" structure (shield on shield, helm on helm, man on man) piles up the sense of crowding.
The granting of only half the prayer signals that Patroclus will not return alive.
Achilles' longing to watch the fighting shows his warlike nature even while he stays out of battle.
The Myrmidons are likened to angry wasps defending their nest, conveying their sudden fury and numbers after long idleness.
Light breaking over a mountain when the storm cloud lifts compares to the Greeks' brief relief as the fire is quenched.
Wolves pouncing on strayed lambs show the Trojans as helpless prey and the Greeks as predators.
Hector, though he sees the tide has turned, still tries to protect his comrades. This shows his courage and sense of duty.
Patroclus's burning wish to kill Hector hints at the confrontation that will lead to his own death.
A flooding autumn storm gives a natural image of the Trojan horses' headlong flight, with a moral note about divine justice.
Thestor hauled from his chariot like a fish on a line makes the killing grimly vivid and demeaning.
The two warriors are compared to screaming vultures, conveying the savagery and noise of their clash.
Juno speaks as the sharp-tongued, politically wary wife, warning Jove that the other gods will resent special treatment.
Sarpedon's fall is compared to a great tree felled for ships, showing his size and the grandeur of his death.
A lion killing a bull adds a second image of violent, struggling death, here suggesting Patroclus' power.
The gruesome picture of the soul leaving with the spear emphasises the physical reality of death.
Patroclus's rush is compared to a hawk scattering small birds, showing his speed and the Trojans' helplessness.
The narrator turns to address Patroclus directly, stressing sympathy and foreshadowing his coming death.
The clash of bronze is compared to woodcutters' axes echoing through the mountains, conveying the noise and relentless labour of battle.
Men swarming round the corpse are likened to flies around full milk-pails, a homely image that makes the scene grimly ordinary.
The narrator hints that Patroclus's pride and Jove's will lead to his death, preparing the reader for his fall.
Patroclus' grim joke about the diving charioteer mocks the dead man, showing his battle fury and arrogance.
Patroclus is likened to a lion struck in the chest while attacking; his own courage destroys him, foreshadowing his death.
Winds battering a forest convey the noise and equal violence of the clashing armies.
The narrator reminds us that Hector too will soon die, tempering his triumph.
Hector as a lion over a boar contrasts with the earlier lion simile for Patroclus, now reversing his role from victor to victim.
The dying Patroclus predicts Hector's death at Achilles' hands, a typical Homeric dying prophecy that sets up the poem's ending.
